Problem Statement
Problem: Algorithms - 36
Suppose that (V, T1) and (V, T2) are two trees defined over a common vertex set V . Prove
that for every edge e in the edge set T1, there exists a corresponding edge f in T2 such
that exchanging these edges preserves the tree structure for both graphs; that is, prove
that (V, (T1 \ {e}) ∪{f}) and (V, (T2 \ {f}) ∪{e}) are both trees.
1

0001 | Solution
0002 | Proof. Let e = {x, y} be an arbitrary edge in T1. Since T1 is a tree, removing e disconnects T1 into
0003 | exactly two components (each of which is itself a tree). Denote these components by A and B, with
0004 | vertex sets VA and VB respectively, such that x ∈VA and y ∈VB. (Equivalently, VA and VB form a
0005 | partition of V , and e was the unique edge of T1 connecting a vertex of VA to a vertex of VB.)
0006 | Now, consider the second tree T2. Since T2 is connected, there is a unique path in T2 from x to y.
0007 | Write this path as
0008 | x = v0 −−v1 −−v2 −−· · · −−vk = y,
0009 | where each vi is a vertex in V and each vi −−vi+1 is an edge in T2. Along this path, we move from
0010 | x ∈VA to y ∈VB, so there must exist some index j where the path first enters VB. In other words, for
0011 | some 1 ≤j ≤k, we have vj−1 ∈VA and vj ∈VB. Consider the edge
0012 | f := { vj−1, vj }.
0013 | This f is an edge of T2 (since it lies on the T2–path from x to y) and, by construction, one endpoint of
0014 | f lies in VA and the other lies in VB. Moreover, f cannot belong to T1 (otherwise T1 would contain an
0015 | edge directly connecting VA and VB other than e, which contradicts the fact that removing e disconnects
0016 | T1).
0017 | Now we exchange the edges e and f between the two graphs. Define the modified edge sets
0018 | E′
0019 | 1 := (T1 \ {e}) ∪{f},
0020 | E′
0021 | 2 := (T2 \ {f}) ∪{e},
0022 | and let T ′
0023 | 1 = (V, E′
0024 | 1) and T ′
0025 | 2 = (V, E′
0026 | 2) be the resulting graphs. We claim that both T ′
0027 | 1 and T ′
0028 | 2 are trees.
0029 | **1. T ′
0030 | 1 is a tree:** T ′
0031 | 1 has |E′
0032 | 1| = |T1| = |V | −1 edges (since we removed one edge from T1 and
0033 | added one edge). We need to check T ′
0034 | 1 is connected and acyclic. By construction, T1 \ {e} consisted
0035 | of two disjoint trees A and B. The new edge f = {vj−1, vj} added to E′
0036 | 1 directly connects a vertex
0037 | vj−1 ∈VA to a vertex vj ∈VB. Thus, f reconnects A and B, making T ′
0038 | 1 a connected graph on all of V .
0039 | Furthermore, T ′
0040 | 1 has no cycles: removing e broke all paths between VA and VB in T1, so there was no
0041 | path in A ∪B between vj−1 and vj; hence adding the single edge f = {vj−1, vj} cannot create a cycle
0042 | (it simply provides the unique route between VA and VB in T ′
0043 | 1). In summary, T ′
0044 | 1 is connected and has
0045 | |V | −1 edges with no cycles, which means T ′
0046 | 1 is a spanning tree on V .
0047 | **2. T ′
0048 | 2 is a tree:** Analogously, T ′
0049 | 2 has |E′
0050 | 2| = |T2| = |V | −1 edges. Since T2 was a tree, removing
0051 | f disconnects T2 into two components. Notably, f = {vj−1, vj} lay on the unique T2–path from x to y,
0052 | so after deleting f, the vertices x and y become separated into different components of T2 \ {f}. The
0053 | added edge e = {x, y} in E′
0054 | 2 precisely reconnects those two components by joining x and y. Thus T ′
0055 | 2 is
0056 | again a connected graph covering all vertices. Moreover, no cycle is created by adding e, since in T2 \{f}
0057 | there was no longer any path between x and y (if there were, T2 would have had two distinct x–y paths
0058 | originally, contradicting the uniqueness of paths in a tree). Therefore T ′
0059 | 2 is also connected and acyclic
0060 | with |V | −1 edges, i.e. a tree.
0061 | In conclusion, for the chosen edge e ∈T1 we have found an edge f ∈T2 such that swapping e and f
0062 | yields two new trees T ′
0063 | 1 and T ′
0064 | 2. This proves the required statement: for every edge e ∈T1, there exists
0065 | an edge f ∈T2 such that (V, (T1 \ {e}) ∪{f}) and (V, (T2 \ {f}) ∪{e}) are both trees.
